analysis.one_liner: Eases cleanup rules for hazardous-waste facilities while strengthening state power over Superfund sites.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 225-188 in January 2014, but the Senate never acted on it, so it never became law.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill changes three environmental laws. First, it removes a rule requiring the EPA to review and update its hazardous-waste regulations at least every three years. Second, it makes it harder for the government to require chemical and energy facilities to prove they can pay for cleaning up their own toxic spills, by letting those facilities count existing state or federal insurance-like coverage toward Superfund requirements and by requiring a detailed report to Congress before any new requirement. Third, it gives states more power over Superfund cleanups and forces federal agencies to clean up their own contaminated sites under the same state rules as everyone else. The House passed it in January 2014, but the Senate never voted on it, so it never became law.
analysis.who_benefits: Industrial facilities that handle hazardous substances gain the most: they would face fewer federal requirements to prove they can pay for disaster cleanup, since existing state or federal coverage would suffice unless the President finds it insufficient. State governments gain more authority over Superfund cleanups and federal facilities in their borders. Communities near facilities storing explosives gain a new requirement that operators notify state emergency commissions about those materials.

how_it_helps.text: Requires federal agencies to clean up their contaminated facilities under the same state requirements as private parties, including state penalties, orders, and land-use controls.
Requires facilities holding flammable or explosive chemicals above a screening threshold to notify the state emergency response commission of what is present and in what quantity.

Requires federal officials to consult with affected states during cleanup selection, gives states credit for removal and oversight costs, and generally prevents adding a site to the National Priorities List over a state's written objection.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people living near hazardous facilities would bear more risk, because weakening mandatory financial responsibility makes it more likely that cleanup costs of a spill fall on taxpayers and the Superfund rather than the facility's owner. Communities near federal sites benefit, though, since federal agencies would lose some immunity from state cleanup requirements.

drawbacks.text: It removes the statutory mandate that EPA review and revise its solid waste regulations at least every three years, so rules governing hazardous waste can sit unreviewed indefinitely unless the agency chooses to revisit them.

It lets chemical and energy facilities satisfy Superfund's financial responsibility requirement with proof of coverage under other state or federal rules, and blocks the President from imposing any new CERCLA financial responsibility requirement without first submitting a detailed report to Congress on why it is needed — a hurdle likely to delay or prevent such requirements.

It bars adding a contaminated site to the Superfund National Priorities List over a state's written objection in most cases, which could leave residents in a state that objects without federal cleanup at a badly polluted site.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill has real merits that should be acknowledged honestly: states get more say over cleanups in their own borders, federal facilities lose their legal shield and must clean up like anyone else, and communities near explosives facilities gain new notification rights. But its core, first-listed provisions run the other way: they make it harder for EPA to require that hazardous-facility industries prove they can pay for their own disasters (Sections 103-105), effectively shifting that risk to Superfund and taxpayers, and they ease the mandate for regular waste-rule review (Section 102). A bill that strengthens accountability in one title while weakening the polluter-pays and review mechanisms in its opening title nets out as a mixed-to-negative trade for the public, with the industry-favoring provisions carrying the most weight.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed the bill 225-188 in January 2014, but the Senate referred it to its environment committee and never voted on it, so it expired when the 113th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House passed the bill on January 9, 2014, on a recorded vote of 225-188.
A Democratic motion to recommit the bill with instructions to preserve the polluter-pays principle failed 188-225, with all voting Republicans opposed and all voting Democrats in favor.
The bill was predominantly a Republican effort: 220 of 232 House Republicans voted yes, while only 5 of 200 House Democrats did.
The Senate received the bill on January 13, 2014, and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, where it remained without further action through the end of the 113th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hazardous-substance facility operators benefited from the bill's failure, since EPA keeps its existing authority — including the three-year regulatory review cycle and its power to impose financial responsibility requirements — while federal agencies keep their existing exemption from certain state cleanup penalties.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hazardous-facility operators; EPA kept its authority

sides.party_line_note: Passage split heavily by party: 220 of 232 Republicans voted yes versus 5 of 200 Democrats, and the Democratic motion to recommit failed 188-225 with all voting Republicans opposed.

industries.industry: Chemical, energy, and hazardous-waste facility owners
industries.note: The bill removes the mandatory three-year review cycle for waste rules and erects new procedural barriers to requiring these industries to carry financial responsibility for hazardous-substance releases. Taxpayers and the Superfund would absorb more of the cost when such facilities cannot pay for a disaster.

States gain consultation rights, cost credits, and leverage over which contaminated sites make the national cleanup list, and can compel federal facilities to comply with state cleanup law. But they also gain the power to block federal cleanup listings, which can work against residents of the objecting state.

industries.industry: Federal agencies (Defense, Energy) with contaminated sites
industries.note: The bill waives sovereign immunity and applies all state response requirements — orders, penalties, and oversight fees — to federal facilities, ending their special treatment. Communities near federal sites stand to benefit.

By making CERCLA financial responsibility requirements harder to issue and by crediting other state and federal coverage, the bill reduces the market for new federally mandated financial-resurance instruments. The bill itself acknowledges this by requiring a report on the financial markets' capacity to supply such instruments.

The agency loses a statutory mandate to revisit waste rules on a fixed cycle and faces a new reporting hurdle before imposing financial responsibility requirements, but gains authority to review other agencies' delegated actions at federal facilities.
